title: Lambdas: functions as values
summary: Write a function inline, store it, and understand captures.

cards.title: A function you can hold
cards.body:
`auto twice = [](int x) { return x * 2; };` creates a small function and stores it in a variable. `twice(4)` returns 8.

- `[]` is the **capture list**: which outside variables the lambda may use.
- `(int x)` are the parameters.
- `{ ... }` is the body.

cards.title: Under the hood: it's an object
cards.body: The compiler turns every lambda into a tiny struct (a **closure**) with an `operator()`. Captured variables become its **members**. Once you see that, every capture rule makes sense.
Look at the sizes: the by-value closure stores an int, the by-reference closure stores a way to reach coins.

cards.question: What does this print?
cards.explain: [n] copied n when the lambda was created (n was 1). Changing n later doesn't affect the copy.

cards.title: mutable
cards.body: By default a lambda can't change its copies (its operator() is const). `mutable` lifts that.

cards.question: What does this print?
cards.explain: The lambda's own copy goes 1, 2, 3. The outer n was never touched: 0.

cards.title: Build it: counters, count_if and a leaderboard
cards.body: Three small functions, all built from lambdas. The counter needs a by-value capture and `mutable`.
